title: Novena for a Desperate or Impossible Case
kicker: 9 days of hope when all seems lost
card: For anyone facing a situation that feels hopeless: 9 days of honest prayer, trust in God’s power and peace in His will.
ogDescription: 9 days of prayer for a desperate or impossible case, through St. Jude, St. Rita and Our Lady, Undoer of Knots.
description: A 9-day Catholic novena for a desperate or impossible case, through St. Jude Thaddeus, St. Rita of Cascia and Our Lady, Undoer of Knots.

epigraph.text: The LORD is near to the brokenhearted, and saves the crushed in spirit.

closingVerse.text: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope.

saints.name: St. Jude Thaddeus
saints.patron: Patron of desperate cases & lost causes
saints.bio: One of the Twelve Apostles, called Thaddaeus by Matthew and Mark. Tradition holds that he preached the Gospel far from home and died a martyr. Christians have long turned to him when all seems lost.
saints.alt: Painting: St. Jude Thaddeus, by Anthony van Dyck

saints.name: St. Rita of Cascia
saints.bio: Born near Cascia in Umbria, she was a wife, mother and widow before entering the Augustinian convent there. Venerated at Cascia since her death, she was canonized in 1900.
saints.alt: Painting: St. Rita of Cascia, from her 15th-century coffin
saints.openingRole: steadfast in hope through every loss

openingPrayer: Heavenly Father, You know the situation we bring before You, the one that feels tangled beyond fixing and heavier than we can carry. We have tried, we are tired, and some days we are close to losing hope. Yet we believe that nothing is impossible for You, and we ask for the grace to trust You whatever the outcome. Today we ask Our Lady, Undoer of Knots; St. Jude Thaddeus, faithful friend in hopeless need; and St. Rita of Cascia, steadfast in hope through every loss, to join their prayers with ours before Your throne, through Christ our Lord.
closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, You hold every tangled thread of our lives. Loosen what binds us, give us light for the next step and peace while we wait, and let Your holy will be done.

tips.p: One person leads each part; all respond pray for us and Amen, and say the closing prayers together. The prayers say “we”; if you pray alone, say “I”.

If you can, go to Confession and attend Mass during these 9 days. Seek wise counsel too: a priest, a trusted friend, and a doctor, counselor or lawyer where needed (Day 4). No novena guarantees a particular outcome, and there is nothing to copy, pass on or publish: simply pray and trust God. Steer clear of fortune-tellers, charms and anyone selling a sure fix. If you ever think of harming yourself, you are not alone: please reach out right away to someone you trust or a crisis helpline.

intentionPlaceholder: Write the situation you are bringing to God, in your own words.
credits: Images: Anthony van Dyck, The Apostle Jude Thaddeus, 1619–21, Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna · Portrait of St Rita on her first coffin, c. 1457, Basilica of St Rita, Cascia (photo: Claudio Roscini). Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

days.title: In My Distress
days.verse: In my distress I called upon the LORD; / to my God I cried for help. / From his temple he heard my voice, / and my cry to him reached his ears.
days.refl: The psalmist does not begin with praise or with a tidy request. He begins in distress, and he says so. That is where many of us stand as we begin this novena: a relationship that has broken, an illness that drags on, a case in court, a loved one far from God, a burden that will not lift. We do not have to feel hopeful before we pray. The first honest prayer is simply to tell God where we are, and ask Him to hear.
days.more: The psalms give words to people who feel they have none. A cry of distress is already a seed of hope: we cry out only to someone we believe can hear. Many turn to St. Jude at the end of their rope. If the darkness brings thoughts of harming yourself, you are not alone: please reach out today to someone you trust or a crisis helpline.
days.prayer: Heavenly Father, in our distress we call upon You. You know this situation better than we do: how long it has lasted, how much it hurts, and how little we can change it by ourselves. We are tired, and some days we are close to giving up. Hear our voice. Through the prayers of St. Jude, faithful friend of those without hope, and of St. Rita, keep us from despair and help us take this one day at a time.
days.step: Write down, in a few honest sentences, the situation you are bringing to God, and keep the page where you pray these nine days.

days.title: Help My Unbelief
days.verse: Immediately the father of the child cried out and said, “I believe; help my unbelief!”
days.refl: The father had watched his son suffer since childhood, and the disciples had already failed to help. When he finally reached Jesus, his faith was a mixture of trust and doubt, and he said so: “I believe; help my unbelief!” Jesus did not send him away for being honest. After a long struggle, our faith may feel just as mixed. We can still bring it, small and shaky as it is, and ask the Lord to strengthen what is weak.
days.more: Faith is first a gift of God (CCC 153). We cannot squeeze it out of ourselves by trying harder; we can ask for it and keep showing up. Tradition remembers St. Rita’s husband as a harsh, quick-tempered man, and her long years of patience with him, praying without seeing change. She kept returning to prayer. A faltering prayer is still a prayer, and God receives it.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, we believe; help our unbelief. After so much waiting, our trust is mixed with doubt and our prayer is often tired. Do not let our weakness keep us from You. Through the prayers of St. Rita, who kept praying through long years of trial, and of St. Jude, strengthen the little faith we have, and give us the courage to keep bringing this need to You, honestly, day after day.
days.step: Pray the father’s words, “I believe; help my unbelief,” slowly three times today, and again whenever doubt or discouragement returns.

days.title: Nothing Is Impossible with God
days.verse: But Jesus looked at them and said to them, “With men this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.”
days.refl: The disciples had just asked who could possibly be saved, and Jesus answered with a look and a promise: what is impossible for us is not impossible for God. The angel told Mary the same thing: “with God nothing will be impossible.” This does not mean God will do whatever we ask. It means no knot is too tight for Him and no situation lies beyond the reach of His mercy, even when we cannot see the way through.
days.more: The devotion to Our Lady, Undoer of Knots, comes from a painting from around 1700 in the church of St. Peter am Perlach in Augsburg, Germany. It shows Mary patiently untying a long ribbon full of knots. It echoes St. Irenaeus, quoted by the Second Vatican Council: the knot of Eve’s disobedience was untied by Mary’s obedience. The future Pope Francis brought the image to Argentina, and from there the devotion spread widely.
days.prayer: Almighty Father, with You nothing is impossible. We bring You the knot we cannot untie: this situation that has defeated our best efforts. Through the prayers of Our Lady, Undoer of Knots, who trusted Your word when the way was hidden, and of St. Jude and St. Rita, loosen what is tangled, open what seems closed, and help us believe that Your mercy can reach even here, and give us patience while You work.
days.step: Picture this situation as a knot, and place it in Mary’s hands with one slow Hail Mary, asking her to bring it to Jesus.

days.title: A Way in the Wilderness
days.verse: Behold, I am doing a new thing; / now it springs forth, do you not perceive it? / I will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert.
days.refl: God spoke these words to His people in exile, when going home seemed impossible. He did not promise to lift them out of the wilderness in a single step; He promised a way through it. Many knots are loosened like that, slowly, one thread at a time. God often opens the way through ordinary means: an honest conversation, a good confessor, a wise friend, a doctor, counselor or lawyer. Seeking help is not a lack of faith. It is how we walk the road He opens.
days.more: St. Jude was one of the Twelve whom Jesus sent out two by two to preach and heal. He did not go alone, and neither do we. Christ often answers prayer through people He places on our path. Asking for help can feel humbling after a long struggle, but it lets others share the weight. Sometimes the first answer to prayer is the right person at the right time.
days.prayer: Lord God, You make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert. Where we see only a dead end, show us the next small step. Send us wise and trustworthy people, and give us the humility to ask for help and accept it. Through the prayers of St. Jude, Your apostle, and of St. Rita and Our Lady, Undoer of Knots, open a path through this wilderness, in Your time and in Your way.
days.step: Name one person who could help with this situation, such as a priest, counselor, doctor or lawyer, and contact them this week.

days.title: Pray & Do Not Lose Heart
days.verse: And he told them a parable, to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart.
days.refl: Jesus told of a widow who kept coming to an unjust judge until he finally heard her case. If even a hard judge listens to persistence, how much more will our Father, who loves us? The lesson is not that we must wear God down, but that we must not wear out. Some cases take a long time. Prayer that keeps coming back, day after day, is never wasted; it keeps our hearts turned toward God while we wait.
days.more: St. Rita’s story, as handed down, tells of the long road of a widow: her husband was killed in a feud, and her two sons died not long after. Near the end of her life, ill and bedridden, she asked a cousin in winter for a rose from her old garden, and one was found in bloom. That is why roses are blessed on her feast: a sign of hope flowering out of season.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You taught us to pray always and not lose heart. When this case drags on and nothing seems to change, keep us faithful in prayer. Guard us from bitterness and from the temptation to give up on You. Through the prayers of St. Rita, who persevered through loss and long waiting, and of St. Jude, help us keep knocking with patience and trust, believing that You hear every prayer.
days.step: Choose a set time to pray each day for the rest of this novena, and keep it even on the days when prayer feels useless.

days.title: Forgiveness Loosens Knots
days.verse: Let all bitterness and wrath and anger and clamor and slander be put away from you, with all malice, and be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.
days.refl: Some knots in our lives are tied by hurt: a betrayal, an injustice, words that cannot be taken back. Bitterness is understandable, but it binds us to the wound. St. Paul asks us to put it away and to forgive as God in Christ forgave us. Forgiveness does not mean pretending the wrong was small, and it does not always mean trusting again or staying in danger. It means handing the debt to God, so the knot in our own heart can begin to loosen.
days.more: Tradition tells that when St. Rita’s husband was murdered, she forgave the men who killed him, and that, fearing her sons would seek revenge, she prayed they would not lose their souls to it. When forgiveness feels impossible, we can begin by asking God for the desire to forgive. It is often a decision we renew many times before our feelings follow. Confession, where we receive God’s mercy ourselves, is often where that grace begins.
days.prayer: Merciful Father, You forgave us in Christ before we ever asked. Where this situation is tangled by hurt, anger or old wounds, free us from bitterness and teach us to forgive as You forgive. Heal what is broken between us and others, where that is possible and safe. Through the prayers of St. Rita, who forgave her husband’s killers, and of St. Jude and Our Lady, Undoer of Knots, soften every hardened heart, beginning with ours.
days.step: If you can, go to Confession this week, and pray by name for one person connected to this situation who has hurt you.

days.title: Heard Through Tears
days.verse: In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard for his godly fear.
days.refl: Jesus Himself prayed with loud cries and tears. In the garden He asked His Father to take the cup away, and the cup was not taken away. Yet He was heard: an angel came to strengthen Him, and beyond the Cross the Father raised Him from the dead. When our prayer is not answered as we hoped, it is not a sign that our faith was too weak or that God does not care. Even the Son’s prayer was answered in a way deeper than the asking.
days.more: Saints, too, knew prayers that were not answered as they asked. St. Paul begged three times to be freed of his affliction, and was given grace instead (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). St. Rita, after long years of loss, bore a painful wound on her forehead in her last years. God did not spare them every sorrow, but He never left them. His answer may differ from ours and still be love.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, in the garden You asked that the cup pass from You, and then gave Yourself to the Father’s will. Teach us to pray the same way: asking with all our hearts, and trusting the Father with the answer. If this burden is not lifted as we hope, give us grace for each day, and keep us from thinking we are forgotten. With St. Jude and St. Rita praying for us, hold us close in every outcome.
days.step: Pray slowly today, as Jesus did in the garden, that the Father’s will be done, offering this situation to Him, and tell Him honestly what you fear about His answer.

days.title: Keep Yourselves in God’s Love
days.verse: But you, beloved, build yourselves up on your most holy faith; pray in the Holy Spirit; keep yourselves in the love of God; wait for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ unto eternal life.
days.refl: The short Letter of Jude, long linked by tradition to the apostle, was written to Christians in a troubled time. Its counsel is simple: build on your faith, pray in the Spirit, keep yourselves in God’s love, and wait for His mercy. That is how we live while a hard situation remains unresolved. We cannot always fix the case, but we can stay close to God within it, and keep our eyes on the mercy that leads to eternal life.
days.more: St. Jude is often painted with a flame above his head, for the Holy Spirit who came upon the apostles at Pentecost, and with an image of Christ’s face on a medallion at his breast. Both point beyond him: the saint we ask for help in hopeless cases leads us to Jesus. The surest place to keep ourselves in God’s love is the Mass, where Christ gives Himself to us.
days.prayer: Holy Spirit, build us up in faith while we wait. When this burden stays and the answer is slow, keep us in the love of God, and do not let us drift from prayer, the sacraments or the people who love us. Through the prayers of St. Jude, friend of all who wait for Your mercy, and of St. Rita and Our Lady, Undoer of Knots, fill us with a hope that reaches all the way to eternal life.
days.step: If you can, go to Mass one extra time this week, and offer this intention to God as the gifts are brought to the altar.

days.title: Gratitude & Trust in God’s Will
days.verse: Now to him who by the power at work within us is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think, to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus to all generations, for ever and ever. Amen.
days.refl: St. Paul ends his prayer with praise for a God who can do far more than all we ask or think. We end these nine days the same way: not by demanding an outcome, but by thanking God and trusting Him with the answer. It may be the very thing we asked, something we did not expect, or the strength to carry what remains. With St. Jude, St. Rita and Our Lady, Undoer of Knots, we place this case in the hands of a faithful Father.
days.more: Looking back over these nine days, we may notice small graces: a conversation that went better than we feared, a clearer next step, an hour of peace, the courage to ask for help. These are signs of God at work. A novena is not a formula that forces a result, and there is nothing to copy or pass on. Trusting God’s will does not mean we stop praying; it means we keep praying in peace.
days.prayer: Father, on this ninth day we thank You for hearing every prayer, and for every grace, seen and unseen, that You have given us. Thank you, Our Lady, Undoer of Knots, St. Jude and St. Rita, for carrying our prayers to Jesus. We place this case in Your loving hands, trusting that You can do far more than we ask or imagine, and that You will give what is truly good for us.
days.step: Write down three graces you noticed during these nine days, and thank God for them together.

printClosing: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing,
so that by the power of the Holy Spirit you may abound in hope.
